Q: How can I insert multiple rows in SQLite? A:

Use:

INSERT INTO TABLE_NAME
            (DATA1, DATA2)
VALUES      (VAL1, VAL2),
            (VAL1, VAL2),
            (VAL1, VAL2),
            (VAL1, VAL2),
            (VAL1, VAL2),
            (VAL1, VAL2),
            (VAL1, VAL2),
            (VAL1, VAL2);

Q: Any way to use k8s exec liveness probes in a distroless container image? A:

You can bake that functionality in your main binary with a command line argument to check if it's health or not. For example if your main app is a binary at /app, do exec command with:

livenessProbe:
  exec:
    command:
      - /app   
      - -healthcheck

and just make sure it returns non-0 if the app is not healthy.

Q: How to set up multi-thread logging to different loggers using QueueListener and QueueHandler A:

To expand on the existing answer with a working implementation -- here's the filter class that actually separates the log streams:

class LoggerNameFilter(logging.Filter):
    def __init__(self, logger_name):
        super().__init__()
        self.logger_name = logger_name

    def filter(self, record):
        return record.name == self.logger_name

# Attach filters to the destination handlers
console_handler.addFilter(LoggerNameFilter('console_logger'))
json_handler.addFilter(LoggerNameFilter('json_logger'))

listener = logging.handlers.QueueListener(
    log_queue, console_handler, json_handler,
    respect_handler_level=True
)

This way each handler only processes records from its intended logger. Without these filters, both handlers receive every record that comes through the queue, which is why you'd see console messages in your JSON file and vice versa.

One other thing -- you're using multiprocessing.Manager().Queue() but since you're only doing threading (ThreadPoolExecutor), not multiprocessing, a regular queue.Queue() works fine and avoids the IPC overhead of a managed queue. The Manager queue is designed for cross-process communication which you don't need here.

Q: Flags or arguments to configure Clangd in Visual Studio Code A:

The behaviour of inserting placeholders for function (and template) arguments can be disabled by passing --function-arg-placeholders=0 to clangd. In Visual Studio Code, you would do this in Visual Studio Code's settings under "clangd.arguments".

Regarding completion of keywords like template and typename, this does work for me out of the box, though note that the completion items have the "snippet" kind, e.g., for template, the item label is "template declaration", but when you choose it, only template is inserted followed by a space, putting the cursor in the right position for you to type the rest of the declaration.

If completion is not working as intended in some specific scenario, I would suggest filing an issue in clangd's issue tracker with details.
